catalog_quote: Nupe ... belongs to the same family as Yoruba, Ibo, Jukon, and other West African languages in which the meaning of a word varies according to the tone upon which it is pronounced. ... Thus be pronounced on the high accent means come. be [middle] again. be [low] to blow. ... As an approximation to the exact sound the following rough rule may be found useful: in any Nupe word the syllable with the highest accent always carries the emphasis. ... This rough rule of laying stress on the highest accent in any word is not quite the same thing as giving each accent its exact sound, but it will prove a great help at the beginning ... [p.16-17:] The three tones on which syllables may be pronounced have been already alluded to. ... (') denotes the Acute or high accent or tone; ... (`) denotes the Grave or low accent; ... When a syllable is unaccented it denotes the Middle accent or tone ... Remem…

new_statements.quote: [p. 11] As an approximation to the exact sound the following rough rule may be found useful : in any Nupe word the syllable with the highest accent always carries the emphasis. Thus in the Nupe word ebi = knife, the emphasis is on the second syllable, as the first is low accent, and the second middle accent; but in ebi = kola nut, the emphasis will be on the first syllable, because it is on a higher accent than the second one, which is on the low accent. [...] This rough rule of laying stress on the highest accent in any word is not quite the same thing as giving each accent its exact sound, but it will prove a great help at the beginning [p. 17] Remember that the syllable with the highest accent in any word bears the stress; emphasize that syllable strongly and you will go far to being understood.

new_statements.relation_note: This is the very source the full catalog record already quotes (the catalog record the primary-stress rule: three-level lexical tone, no positional stress rule, learner's heuristic that emphasis falls on the highest-toned syllable). Re-reading confirms the wording verbatim and pins the pages (p. 11 and p. 17 by the running headers 'CHARACTERISTICS 11' and 'THE ACCENTS 17'; the catalog's 'pp. 10-12 / 16-17' locators span the same passages). Agrees with the catalog classification tonal.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Nupe is a three-level tone language (acute/high, unmarked/middle, grave/low, plus rare circumflex and inverted-circumflex contours, p. 17) in which tone is lexically contrastive (be 'come' / 'again' / 'to blow', p. 11). The only statement about stress is a learner's heuristic: the syllable carrying the highest tone in a word is the one that bears the stress/emphasis, so perceived prominence is a function of tone, not of position. No positional word-stress rule is given.
new_statements.exceptions: The authors themselves call the rule 'rough' and 'an approximation', explicitly distinct from giving each tone its exact pitch (p. 11). Appendix note (near the end of the grammar): 'Some words seem to have an accent half way between the middle and the acute accent, and to be pronounced on a higher note than the ordinary middle accent' (e.g. bagi 'man', lefi 'sin, fault'), unmarked. Sentence-level tone changes ('The False Accentuation', 'Raising of Tone in Negative Sentences') are described as temporary tonal changes due to tone sequence, not stress.
new_statements.identity_note: Banfield & Macintyre 1915 (pp. 10-11) name the dialects Bini, Gbedigi, Benu, Ebagi, Cekpan, Kiadia and Kusopaci and say 'the best and purest Nupe is spoken' in the Trans-Kaduna district 'but the differences are not very great'; the grammar itself describes Nupe generally (missionary usage centred on the Bida emirate) without tying its tone/stress remarks to one dialect.

audit.reasoning: Quote check: every fragment of the deciding quotation is present in the held Banfield & Macintyre 1915 djvu text at pp.10-12 and 16-17 and in the held George 1970 SAL text at pp.100-101, verbatim modulo scanned noise. The classification (tonal: H/M/L + rising/falling, no positional stress; 'stress' only as a learner's heuristic = highest-toned syllable) is exactly what Banfield says and is consistent with George 1970. Web check and downloads: Kandybowicz 2004 (UCLWPL 16, instrumental pitch-track study) explicitly says 'Nupe is not a pitch accent language' and analyses only lexical tone; Blench 2013 sec. 2.3 gives three level tones + two glides for all Nupoid; Kandybowicz 2006 diss gives only tone-marking conventions. No source seen posits word stress for Nupe. The primary citation is a 1915 pedagogical grammar, but it is backed by a held 1970 phonology article and now a 2004 instrumental study

sources.citation: Kandybowicz, Jason (2004). Nupe tonology and the categorical identity of verb copy tones: a pilot experimental study. UCL Working Papers in Linguistics 16: 17-53.
sources.quote: Instrumental (pitch-track) study of Nupe lexical tone (H, M, L, rising) on one speaker; states 'Nupe is not a pitch-accent language' and that lexical tone is preserved under sentence intonation apart from declination and IP-final boundary effects. No word stress is posited anywhere in the paper.
sources.locator: p.17 fn.1 (tone marking: high = acute, low = grave, mid unmarked, contours as combinations); p.21 ('lexical tone is preserved in the language.. Additionally, Nupe is not a pitch accent language.')

sources.quote: 'All Nupoid languages presently studied have at least five surface tones, three level tones and two glides.
